🇲🇽🌊 <u>MEXICO GOES ALL-IN ON SARGASSUM: 2 BILLION PESOS, MORE SHIPS, A CIRCULAR ECONOMY</u>

While a record sargassum surge floods the Caribbean — 90,538 tons a day floating offshore, 27 times the historical average and four times last year — Mexico isn't waiting for anyone to save its beaches. The federal government is investing 2 billion pesos to intercept the algae at sea: more Navy sargassum vessels (about 250 million pesos each), 50 km of containment barriers, and 150 scientists working to turn the plague into biogas, biofertilizer and bioplastics at a new circular-economy hub in Puerto Morelos.

"This year more sargassum arrived at the beaches of Quintana Roo, and the scientists have to explain why — and also how to recycle the algae," Sheinbaum said. Climate change made the mess; Mexico is building the response.

♻️🌊 From plague to product: Mexican firms already export sargassum-based fertilizer. "That sargassum becomes organic powder that can be reused. There are already companies in Quintana Roo recycling it into fertilizer — and it's even being exported for agricultural production." — President Claudia Sheinbaum Some 150 scientists from Semarnat and the Science Ministry are working on sargassum recycling; companies already produce biofertilizer, biochar and biogas. Fonatur will build 4 final-disposal sites with the state government.

🗳️📺 "There has never been more freedom of expression than now — I can assure you." "There is a TV network that dedicates 24 hours to speaking badly of the Government. When have we ever asked for censorship, or for a host to be removed?" — President Claudia Sheinbaum Responding to criticism of the new audience-rights guidelines for concessioned media — published for public consultation and, she stressed, built by consensus. Via Q&A press coverage; full stenographic transcript pending.

🤝🌊 "Mexico will be, without a doubt, the world leader in sargassum management." "This is the most complete response sargassum has ever received anywhere in the world. No more isolated efforts — today there is one single effort, and it belongs to all of Mexico." — Iván Chávez, Grupo Vidanta After years of every hotel and municipality fighting alone, hoteliers now sit at one table with the Navy, federal and state governments and scientists — sharing techniques, barriers and data.

🏆🌊 2025 and 2026 are the two biggest sargassum-collection years in Quintana Roo's history. "Attention to sargassum is no longer just an immediate response — it is a permanent State policy." — Mexican Navy, strategy briefing 96,151 tons collected so far in 2026 — already more than all of 2025 (92,782 tons). A 2,635.6M-peso expansion adds 2 oceanic vessels, 6 semi-oceanic ones, 35 km of barriers, early-warning monitoring and a dock in Puerto Juárez.

🛡️🌊 The Navy's mission: catch the sargassum before it touches the beach. "We have to invert this graph: collect mainly at sea, so it doesn't reach the beaches, and give the sargassum a final destination in industry." — Adm. Raymundo Morales, Navy Secretary A first 768.7M-peso stage lifts at-sea collection capacity to 1,870 tons/day: 2 tugboats, 6 coastal sargassum vessels, more dynamic barriers and ~50 km of containment barriers in the five most critical zones.

📈🌊 Sargassum in 2026: 27 times the historical average. "In 2026 it was 4 times more than in 2025. And we have 27 times more than the historical average. This has been a really difficult, atypical year." — Alicia Bárcena, Environment Secretary Up to 90,538 tons of sargassum per day are drifting in the Mexican Caribbean; about 10% reaches Quintana Roo's coasts. Mexico will host an EU-backed international sargassum summit in Cancún on October 1-2, with Japan offering support with collection vessels.
